newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian presidential poll overshadowed by crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian presidential poll overshadowed by crisis.

text.p: Bulgarian presidential candidates began their final week of campaigning on Sunday, battling for the attention of voters more concerned with the country's grave economic and social crisis.
"The coming winter will be one of the hardest for this country," Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, candidate of the ruling Bulgarian Socialist Party, told Reuters in an interview.

"It will be difficult because of the energy prices, the bread problem and the unemployment. More so because it coincides with the actual start of radical structural reform. This economic reform is the basis for adapting to the standards of the modern world and is our only way to join that world."

Monthly inflation is approaching 20 percent and the average monthly wage is worth the equivalent of $55. The central bank must find money for nuclear fuel, coal and wheat from its dwindling foreign currency reserves to avert bread and power shortages during the coming Balkan winter.

Many Bulgarians have told pollsters they are too disillusioned with politicians to bother voting, but Petar Stoyanov, candidate of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), said he hoped dissatisfaction with the Socialists would bring people out to vote for him.
Opinion polls have shown him slightly ahead of Marazov but still short of an absolute majority in the first round.
"A political victory is valuable only if it leads to an improvement in the standard of living," he said.

"We have to discuss what action is necessary to secure the survival of some Bulgarians during the coming winter. Those people will be forced to choose between two vital components -- food and heating."

The central bank raised its main interest rate to a record high of 300 percent last month in a bid to stabilise the lev and curb inflation. Economists say the shock treatment is showing signs of working and on Thursday the bank cut the rate to 240 percent.

Two televised debates between the two main candidates have concentrated on national security and foreign policy, issues more relevant to the office of president but somewhat distant from the real concerns of Bulgaria's 8.5 million people.

Under its post-communist constitution, Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic in which the president's powers are limited to vetoing legislation once, appointing ambassadors and some state officials and commanding the armed forces.
Stoyanov said he wanted to integrate the former Warsaw pact state into the European Union and NATO, but Marazov said he would like to put these issues to a referendum.
"The Bulgarian people are still not aware of the advantages of NATO membership. They are not sure whether NATO would guarantee security," Marazov said.
"I would propose to hold a referendum on NATO membership which must be preceded by a broad discussion on its advantages and disadvantages."

Outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev, who lost an American-style UDF party primary in June and is not seeking re-election, has publicly criticised the Socialist government, but Stoyanov said that, if elected, he would support any Socialist initiative to end the country's crisis.
"I am ready for any compromise if it contributes to the interests of Bulgaria," he said.
A total of 13 candidates are contesting Sunday's poll. If no one wins a majority in the first round, a second round is scheduled a week later.
